3.text: natives are not so eager for liquor as formerly, because their means of buying

4.text: have rather diminished, and new and varied wants have been acquired, which

5.text: they are bent upon satisfying above everything else. However, quantities of

6.text: rum, put into bladders and small gut bags, are carried inland far from Indian

7.text: Point and East Cape. In the traffic in the Hare Mountains it even formed

8.text: one of the most important items bartered by the Chukchee to the Russians.

9.text: At present similar transactions take place at Mariinsky Post every time the

10.text: Chukchee and Eskimo traders come from the north. Thus the relations of

11.text: the Russians and the natives toward each other are quite reversed, as often

12.text: happens in remote parts of Siberia. The Russians pay in tea, tobacco, etc.,

13.text: also in live dogs, which last are considered to be much better than the Chuk-

14.text: chee race, and are taken every year from Anadyr to northern native villages.

15.text: The guns sold now by the whalers are chiefly Winchester rifles of 44,

16.text: 45.60, or 45.70 calibre, for the most part second-hand. They also sell cheap

17.text: shotguns, and reloading-tools for both kinds of guns. At present all the

18.text: natives on both the Arctic and Pacific shores are armed with these rifles, and

19.text: use them for every kind of hunting. At Indian Point alone the number of

20.text: fire-arms in 1901 was over four hundred in a population of four hundred and

21.text: forty. The Reindeer Chukchee eastward from the Kolyma also have many

22.text: Winchester rifles; while those of the western tundra and of Omolon still use

23.text: firelocks, with only a small number of second-hand Berdan rifles sold by the

25.text: Wheat flour has become an article of regular consumption on the Pacific

26.text: shore, especially in times when seals are scarce. Then, according to the

27.text: assertion of the natives, it is their only means of keeping off famine. In

28.text: truth, during the spring of 1901, people in the village of Iˊᵋen, on Plover

29.text: Bay, and also at Indian Point, lived chiefly on flour cakes baked with a little

30.text: oil. The same spring, at Indian Point alone, about five hundred sacks of

31.text: flour (forty-four pounds to the sack) were bought from the whalers. On the

32.text: whole coast, about twenty-five hundred sacks of flour — rather more than

33.text: less — are sold every summer. Among the Reindeer Chukchee, cakes made

34.text: of wheat flour form one of the most relished dainties, while rye flour is little

35.text: cared for, even in the vicinity of the Russian settlements.

36.text: Besides these provisions and wares, the natives willingly buy second-hand

37.text: whaling-boats, small whaling-guns, exploding-harpoons, and also mineral oil

38.text: and oil-stoves; in 1901 even Primus lamps, ships’ compasses, the use of which

39.text: is well known to the Eskimo at least, etc., were traded in.

40.text: In 1882, Kuvaˊr, the richest trader of Indian Point, tried to buy a schooner

41.text: for the purpose of carrying on whaling and trading on a larger scale.
